# What does this PR do?

As per #13446 `trust_remote_code` fails under several circumstances:

- `pretrained_model_name_or_path` as Hub repo A and `custom_pipeline` as Hub repo B, `trust_remote_code` is bypassed and remote code runs from repo B
```python

from diffusers import DiffusionPipeline

DiffusionPipeline.from_pretrained(
    "google/ddpm-cifar10-32", custom_pipeline="XManFromXlab/diffuser-custom-pipeline", trust_remote_code=False
)

```
- `pretrained_model_name_or_path` as local directory and `custom_pipeline` as Hub repo B, `trust_remote_code` is **never checked** and remote code runs from repo B
```python

from diffusers import DiffusionPipeline
from huggingface_hub import snapshot_download

snapshot_path = snapshot_download(repo_id="google/ddpm-cifar10-32")
DiffusionPipeline.from_pretrained(
    snapshot_path, custom_pipeline="XManFromXlab/diffuser-custom-pipeline", trust_remote_code=False
)

```
- `pretrained_model_name_or_path` as local directory with custom components, `trust_remote_code` is never checked
```python

from diffusers import DiffusionPipeline
from huggingface_hub import snapshot_download

snapshot_path = snapshot_download(repo_id="hf-internal-testing/tiny-sdxl-custom-components")
pipeline = DiffusionPipeline.from_pretrained(
    snapshot_path, trust_remote_code=False
)
assert pipeline.config.unet == ("diffusers_modules.local.my_unet_model", "MyUNetModel")
assert pipeline.config.scheduler == ("diffusers_modules.local.my_scheduler", "MyScheduler")

```

This moves `trust_remote_code` checks into `get_cached_module_file` where the actual custom module loading takes place. `trust_remote_code` is passed from several code paths for complete coverage.

I've added 3 separate `ValueError` in `get_cached_module_file` to account for the different sources of remote code: `local`, `git` and `hub`. `git` path could be considered trusted as these are from `https://huggingface.co/datasets/diffusers/community-pipelines-mirror`, `hub` path covers "custom pipelines" and `local` path is reached for "custom components" (these are added to the `allowed files` in `download` so become local files).

With PR the above 3 cases are resolved:
```
The repository for XManFromXlab/diffuser-custom-pipeline contains custom code in pipeline.py which must be executed to correctly load the model. You can inspect the repository content at https://hf.co/XManFromXlab/diffuser-custom-pipeline/blob/main/pipeline.py.
Please pass the argument `trust_remote_code=True` to allow custom code to be run.
```
```
The repository for XManFromXlab/diffuser-custom-pipeline contains custom code in pipeline.py which must be executed to correctly load the model. You can inspect the repository content at https://hf.co/XManFromXlab/diffuser-custom-pipeline/blob/main/pipeline.py.
Please pass the argument `trust_remote_code=True` to allow custom code to be run.
```
```
ValueError: The directory C:\Users\user\.cache\huggingface\hub\models--hf-internal-testing--tiny-sdxl-custom-components\snapshots\ce2b9d3f819e7791f53053646ebe37d7e87d73d3\unet contains custom code in my_unet_model.py which must be executed to correctly load the model. You can inspect the file content at C:\Users\user\.cache\huggingface\hub\models--hf-internal-testing--tiny-sdxl-custom-components\snapshots\ce2b9d3f819e7791f53053646ebe37d7e87d73d3\unet\my_unet_model.py.
Please pass the argument `trust_remote_code=True` to allow custom code to be run.
```


Fixes #13446


## Who can review?

Anyone in the community is free to review the PR once the tests have passed. Feel free to tag
members/contributors who may be interested in your PR.

body:
Found another case, I will discuss it further here to avoid too much noise on the PR:

- `pretrained_model_name_or_path` as local directory with custom components, `trust_remote_code` is never checked
```python

from diffusers import DiffusionPipeline
from huggingface_hub import snapshot_download

snapshot_path = snapshot_download(repo_id="hf-internal-testing/tiny-sdxl-custom-components")
pipeline = DiffusionPipeline.from_pretrained(
    snapshot_path, trust_remote_code=False
)
assert pipeline.config.unet == ("diffusers_modules.local.my_unet_model", "MyUNetModel")
assert pipeline.config.scheduler == ("diffusers_modules.local.my_scheduler", "MyScheduler")

```

This one is particularly interesting. It is fairly common, especially in the wider community and those who prefer local files, to download a Hub repo and then use that local directory with `from_pretrained`. The second case mentioned in the PR and in the comment above would still require a user to specify a malicious repo as `custom_pipeline`, this case does not, simply loading the local directory that contains malicious custom components would run the malicious code.

A malicious actor could reupload a popular model and insert custom components, this would be particularly effective if the chosen model was access gated as many users would opt for the non-gated version.
This would also affect DDUF files, although they are [underutilized](https://github.com/huggingface/huggingface_hub/issues/3716#issuecomment-3822410259) at present.
Thanks, all, for the discussions! I just reviewed the PR from @hlky. I will let @DN6 do a review as well.

Thanks for reviewing and addressing the issue. I really appreciate the effort from the team. I’m reaching out to ask whether it would be possible to request or assign a CVE for this issue. This work is part of an ongoing academic research on security risks in ML ecosystems, and having a CVE would help us better track and reference the vulnerability in a standardized way. Thanks again for your time and support.

My two cents here is that it's kind of a gray area. Using custom_pipeline is actually a "use remote code" enabling feature, but at the same time you're disabling trust_remote_code. These are two separate mechanisms and the docs don't explicitly say one gates the other.

Also in the https://huggingface.co/docs/diffusers/using-diffusers/custom_pipeline_overview we have a warning with:

  ▎ "you should still inspect the Hub pipeline code and make sure it is safe"

This is something we should fix and it's being done in the PR, but the users should always check what custom pipeline or component are they using instead of blindly relying on this.

My doubt here is that if the user is explicitly using a feature that runs remote code, does this fall as a CVE?

IIUC, the user does *not* have to decide to use remote code but rather has to decide to use remote weights. Old Diffusers versions are very common in everything from production libraries to research code, which means that publicizing this risk is particularly important now that malicious actors have easy access to an exploit POC.

using custom pipelines is actually using remote code, diffusers doesn't ship with custom pipelines, you're confusing the core pipelines with the custom ones, if people don't understand that, maybe we need to be more clear in the docs with this. The only difference is that by default diffusers looks in the custom pipelines (github mirror) if it matches a certain criteria, but you can actually pass a local pipeline or another repo id with a pipeline as OP did.

So to be clear again, for the user to be affected by this, they need to knowingly and actively pass a custom "repo id" with a custom pipeline that they don't know what it does even with a red note in our docs that says that they should inspect the hub pipeline.

> you're confusing the core pipelines with the custom ones

Oops, not the first time I've shot the wrong horse thief. My bigger-picture comment about a CVE remains, however. This sort of oversight is ripe for supply chain exploitation along the lines of the recent LiteLLM attack:

- Downstream library uses a custom pipeline with `trust_remote_code=False`
- Malicious actor takes over the remote HF repository and inserts a malware payload
- Anyone looking at the downstream library code would be forgiven for thinking that the malware would not execute

that's actually the main issue, it doesn't make sense to use a `custom pipeline` without allowing the use of remote code, that pipeline won't run. If people before the fix have this, then it's really weird and doesn't make any sense, and it will break whatever they are using it for because it will fail to load with the pipeline.

This doesn't fix a security issue, it fixes a weird combination of trying to use remote code but not allowing it at the same time.

The security issue will still be present, people that use `custom pipelines` blindly using remote code that they don't know what it does or if the URL exist, will still have the security problem.

Got it (I hope). If a `custom_pipeline` by its nature involves running remotely hosted code, perhaps it would be helpful to rename it to something like `remote_pipeline` so that the feature is better described?

probably it can help but that's a breaking change for all the people that are using `custom_pipeline` so not sure if it's doable for something like this.

The PR is good for this though, because people that just use `custom_pipeline` will have to enable also `trust_remote_code` or it won't work, but this is also a breaking change, all the ones that are running actually will fail when they update diffusers with that PR merged.
It would have to be a two-stage process, making the change with a deprecation warning first and then removing the old nomenclature in a later version.

Thanks for the discussion. I agree that this falls into a gray area from a feature-design perspective. However, from a security standpoint, `trust_remote_code` is the only explicit signal of the user’s trust boundary, and it should be enforced consistently across all remote code paths.
In this case, even though `custom_pipeline` is intended to load external code, the fact that code execution occurs with `trust_remote_code=False` still breaks that trust boundary.

For comparison, the transformers library has a similar option called `custom_generate`, which can load `custom_generate/generate.py` from another remote model repository.  The code looks like: 

```python
gen_out = model.generate(**inputs, left_padding=5, custom_generate="transformers-community/custom_generate_example", trust_remote_code=True)
```

transformers explicitly requires `trust_remote_code=True` with `custom_generate`option. 

```text
            trust_remote_code (`bool`, *optional*):
                Whether or not to allow for custom models defined on the Hub in their own modeling files. This option
                should only be set to `True` for repositories you trust and in which you have read the code, as it will
                execute code present on the Hub on your local machine.
```

Here are more details if you are interested: [load_custom_generate() in transformers](https://github.com/huggingface/transformers/blob/a29df2d916e3b820aecd19d3b5a877abc523ba3c/src/transformers/generation/utils.py#L433), example repository: [transformers-community/custom_generate_example](https://huggingface.co/transformers-community/custom_generate_example).

https://github.com/huggingface/diffusers/issues/13446#issuecomment-4231839537

This case does not involve the user passing `custom_pipeline` - it requires no user interaction other than pre-downloading the Hub repo which is very common.

> This case does not involve the user passing `custom_pipeline` - it requires no user interaction other than pre-downloading the Hub repo which is very common.

In which case it deserves a CVE.

yeah, so that's why I'm not completely sure about it.

A rough example of the same is that you enable your firewall to protect your computer, but you then go to some shady site and install something that when installing it opens a port and installs a remote terminal allowing an external intruder to hack your computer, do you blame your firewall and open a CVE with this? 

The firewall is for preventing this but at the same time you installed something that bypasses it, it is the same scenario, you set the `trust_remote_code` to False but at the same time you're trying to explicitly load remote code.

Just to be clear, this is something that we need to fix to ensure the best for the users, but what I'm not sure about, is if it's worth of a CVE or not, when the clear intent of the user is to load remote code.

> This case does not involve the user passing custom_pipeline - it requires no user interaction other than pre-downloading the Hub repo which is very common.

yeah, I was discussing more the OP issue. But still, I also think it's not clear if it's worth of a CVE because of the user intention.

So the flow will be:

if the user sets `trust_remote_code` to `False` and tries to use a model repo with arbitrary code, it will fail and it won't download the code, all good.

So to be able to do this, they have to either download the repo with git, hf download, manual download, etc, but not with diffusers. Then they have to use diffusers with their already downloaded model with arbitrary code and then this will trigger even with `trust_remote_code` set to `False`, at this point, its practically not remote code but local code though, is this worth a CVE?

P.S.: This is a genuine question, if most people think this is a CVE, then it is I guess.

> yeah, I was discussing more the OP issue. But still, I also think it's not clear if it's worth of a CVE because of the user intention

The risk is not so much a user choosing to access a shady repository, but rather a repeat of the [LiteLLM attack](https://blog.pypi.org/posts/2026-04-02-incident-report-litellm-telnyx-supply-chain-attack/) where a malicious actor seizes control of, and then publishes new code to, a previously benign repository. All current versions of Diffusers would silently allow  that code to run once it is downloaded in the normal course of end-user usage, even, or perhaps especially!, when the application developers had no intention for custom code to be run. As @hlky says, pre-downloading checkpoints prior to inference is a common scenario.

Some useful background reading about the LiteLLM attack can be found [here](https://cybernews.com/security/critical-litellm-supply-chain-attack-sends-shockwaves/).

I know the LiteLLM case and other supply chain attacks (they are not new), but I don't think it applies here, those are real no user interactions attacks and also those aren't CVEs on the libraries that use a compromised dependency, practically there's nothing you can do except to make your library completely locked to verified versions or to remove any dependencies and code them again in your project, both are not real things you can do in the AI space.

We agree then that the OP case is not worth a CVE then, the one in debate is the one where you have the compromised model from before hand.

For that one, you can probably ask an expert? What I'm not sure, is that this is not a vulnerability made with this library, it needs for two things to happen at the same time from outside of diffusers:

- For an external repository to be compromised even with hf security scans
- At the same time, the user has to download via other means the repository and then try to use it with diffusers.

Note: if the user downloaded the model and the repository gets compromised after that, if the user doesn't update the model manually, and they use it with diffusers, it's safe, diffusers won't update the model with the compromised code.

Also I don't think it's that common for this to happen as most users, use diffusers to download them, maybe more advanced users do this, but this are just suppositions, we need real data to corroborate or refute this assumption which we don't have.

But at this stage, if done this way, it's not wrong to be treated as a "not remote code", because it's actually in the user's machine and maintained by them no?

> We agree then that the OP case is not worth a CVE then

I don't agree. `trust_remote_code` is presented as a protection mechanism so it should cover all cases. See [CWE-693](https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/693.html). Afaik using `custom_pipeline` is not explicitly stated to override `trust_remote_code`, regardless of whether passing a `custom_pipeline` can be considered implicit trust if an explicit trust protection mechanism exists that should take priority - otherwise the protection mechanism might as well not exist.

> you can probably ask an expert

HF has a security team, no?

> is that this is not a vulnerability made with this library, it needs for two things to happen at the same time from outside of diffusers

User interaction is the case for many vulnerabilities, do we need to find a zero-click RCE for a vulnerability to be valid?

> I don't think it's that common for this to happen as most users

I took a quick look at the first page of Issues and PRs, of those with code examples that involve models/pipelines, around half use local directories, this also mirrors my intuition having seen many issues and PRs here over the years. Perhaps you could check the metrics Diffusers collects if it's covered, but I don't think that's necessary, it's not much of a leap to assume users do use local directories and it doesn't make the issue go away by pretending they don't.

> it's not wrong to be treated as a "not remote code"

Is "remote" really the right distinction here? Surely the actual intent, and what a reasonable person would expect, is "third party" code - anything that is not a part of Diffusers. The source of the code, or more accurately, the model/pipeline repo, as that's what we actually download, is irrelevant IMO.

User downloads pipeline -> Diffusers executes third party code without consent

It is that simple.

I don't want this to be a heated discussion, I'm just stating that it's not crystal clear that this is a CVE or not, hence the question.

I'm just answering and discussing about the question OP made [here](https://github.com/huggingface/diffusers/issues/13446#issuecomment-4269221559):

By no means I have or want any authority to prevent someone from opening a CVE so feel free to open it all you want.

I'll just add that a firewall doesn't work if you use `block all incoming connections`  when you also explicitly open a port or install an app that does it, it is also that simple.

I won't engage in a discussion that tries to ridicule the other side, so I'll stop here.

Perhaps [publishing a GHSA](https://docs.github.com/en/code-security/how-tos/report-and-fix-vulnerabilities/fix-reported-vulnerabilities/publishing-a-repository-security-advisory) would be sufficient? This would ensure that downstream users are notified via Dependabot and does not require a CVE to be assigned.

Here is the CVSS 3.1 string I get when trying to stay cautious about the overall impact:

`CVSS:3.1/AV:L/AC:H/PR:L/UI:R/S:C/C:L/I:L/A:L`

- Attack vector: Local, because "the attacker’s path is via read/write/execute capabilities"
- Attack complexity: High, because "a successful attack depends on conditions beyond the attacker's control"
- Privileges required: Low, because we can assume that an attack would primarily impact "only settings and files owned by a user"
- User interaction: Required, because the user must access an impacted repository or DDUF file
- Scope: Changed, because the "vulnerability can affect resources beyond [...] the vulnerable component"
- Confidentiality: Low, because it is not clear that "all resources within the impacted component" would be "divulged to the attacker"
- Integrity: Low, because it is not clear that there would be "a total loss of integrity, or a complete loss of protection"
- Availability: Low, because "the attacker does not have the ability to completely deny service to legitimate users"

Severity: 5.0 (moderate)

If the assumptions about confidentiality and integrity are wrong, and both of these impacts rise to High, the severity increases to 7.4 (high).

I will just add:

`trust_remote_code` should be understood as the explicit consent boundary for executing third-party code while loading a pipeline artifact. A model repo / local snapshot is closer to an active document or project file than to a plain weights file: it may contain data, config, and executable extensions. The relevant security property is therefore not whether the artifact is "remote" or already on disk, but whether loading it can cause Diffusers to execute third-party code. In the same way that Word should not run embedded macros just because a document was opened from a local folder instead of downloaded directly, Diffusers should not execute custom pipeline/component code unless the user explicitly opts in. This is especially important because Diffusers is clearly intended to support both Hub-backed and local-only workflows, as shown by options like `local_files_only`, so the trust boundary cannot coherently depend on transport path.

I also looked at the custom-component detection logic more closely. There is another inconsistency: `_get_custom_components_and_folders()` skips component entries whose first tuple element is not a string, so a crafted `model_index.json` can bypass the "contains custom components" determination in the Hub `download()` path. I verified this with a PoC using `"tokenizer": [1, "CLIPTokenizer"]`, which bypasses the custom-component check but later crashes during loading with `TypeError: attribute name must be string, not 'int'` when Diffusers reaches `hasattr(pipelines, library_name)`. So this particular PoC is not a demonstrated execution bypass, but it does prove that the `trust_remote_code` detection invariant is broken: a repo can be classified as not containing custom components even though the configuration has already stepped outside the assumptions of the trusted path.

What makes this concerning is how narrow the gap is between this malformed-config PoC and a full bypass. In this case execution is only prevented because later code still happens to assume `library_name` is a real string and fails early on type handling. If only a handful of lines in the dynamic-loading path were written slightly differently, for example, by coercing the value to a string while constructing the candidate filename instead of relying on strict string-only operations, the same inconsistency could plausibly have become a complete `trust_remote_code` bypass. Even where this PoC does not yet produce code execution, it shows that `trust_remote_code` is not backed by a robust, consistently enforced notion of what counts as third-party executable content.

For reference, these lines are the difference between a full bypass in this PoC. Changes like this could plausibly arise either through routine maintenance/refactoring or through deliberate action.

issue.body:
**Is your feature request related to a problem? Please describe.**
This FR relates to the recent discovery of a [security issue](https://github.com/huggingface/diffusers/issues/13446) in Diffusers, which sometimes results in the execution of custom pipeline code regardless of user intention. In addition to fixing those specific flaws in Diffusers, it may be helpful for this library to warn users when:

- There is Python code, **and**
- The code contains risky functions

**Describe the solution you'd like**
Adopt guidelines similar to ComfyUI's [Security Standards for custom nodes](https://docs.comfy.org/registry/standards#security-standards) and warn users when Python code is download from the Hub, or accessed from DDUF files!, that:

- Imports `requests` or similar libraries used to download extra files, or
- Manually references Pickletensor files (PTH/BIN), or
- Runs subprocesses, or
- Uses `eval` or `exec` calls

**Describe alternatives you've considered**
Scanning of legacy Pickletensor files using [Picklescan](https://github.com/mmaitre314/picklescan) by default, with an opt-out, may also be worthwhile considering. However, this library is maintained by a third party.

**Additional context**
cc @hlky

# Vulnerabilidades Identificadas no Pacote `diffusers` (pip)

Este pacote possui **2** alerta(s) de segurança ativo(s).

## CVEs Associados
`CVE-2026-44513`, `CVE-2026-45804`

## GHSA IDs
`GHSA-7wx4-6vff-v64p`, `GHSA-98h9-4798-4q5v`

## Alertas Detalhados

### 1. Diffusers: TOCTOU Trust Remote Code Bypass (CVE-2026-45804)
**Severidade:** HIGH

**Manifesto:** `botmodels/requirements.txt`

**Descrição:**
## Background

This vulnerability is found in the `diffusers` package - the `transformers`-equivalent library for diffusion models.

It is found in the `DiffusionPipeline.from_pretrained` flow, which is used to load a pipeline from the HuggingFace Hub.

This function has a `trust_remote_code` guard: if the repository’s `model_index.json` references a custom pipeline class defined in a `.py` file in the repo, the load is blocked unless `trust_remote_code=True` is explicitly passed:

```
ValueError: The repository for attacker/repo contains custom code in pipeline.py
which must be executed to correctly load the model. You can inspect the repository
content at https://hf.co/attacker/repo/blob/main/pipeline.py.
Please pass the argument `trust_remote_code=True` to allow custom code to be run.
```

The vulnerability allows arbitrary code execution through the custom pipeline flow from a Hub repo, with no `custom_pipeline` or `trust_remote_code` kwargs passed. The `from_pretrained` call succeeds and returns a functional pipeline.

---

## Naive Flow

`DiffusionPipeline.from_pretrained` begins by popping all relevant arguments from `kwargs` into local variables, then calls `DiffusionPipeline.download()` to fetch the repo files:

```python
# pipeline_utils.py:853
cached_folder = cls.download(
    pretrained_model_name_or_path,
    ...
    custom_pipeline=custom_pipeline,
    trust_remote_code=trust_remote_code,
    ...
)
```

Inside `download()`, `model_index.json` is fetched first as a standalone file via `hf_hub_download`:

```python
# pipeline_utils.py:1636
config_file = hf_hub_download(
    pretrained_model_name,
    cls.config_name,
    ...
)
config_dict = cls._dict_from_json_file(config_file)
```

This config is used to detect custom pipeline code and enforce the trust check:

```python

    custom_pipeline = config_dict["_class_name"][0]

load_pipe_from_hub = custom_pipeline is not None and f"{custom_pipeline}.py" in filenames

if load_pipe_from_hub and not trust_remote_code:
```

After the check passes, `snapshot_download` then fetches all files and saves them to disk:

```python

    pretrained_model_name,
    ...
```

```python
# pipeline_loading_utils.py:974
def _resolve_custom_pipeline_and_cls(folder, config, custom_pipeline):
    custom_class_name = None

        custom_pipeline = os.path.join(folder, f"{custom_pipeline}.py")

    return custom_pipeline, custom_class_name
```

## The Vulnerability

`hf_hub_download` and `snapshot_download` are two independent HTTP calls to the Hub, both resolving the repository’s default branch (if `revision=None`) to its current HEAD at call time. There is no atomicity guarantee between them - if the repository is updated between the two calls, they will resolve to different commits and download different content, with no warning displayed to the user.

The trust check in `download()` operates on the content fetched by `hf_hub_download` (commit A). The `snapshot_download` call that immediately follows can silently fetch a newer commit (commit B). The config in the newer commit will be the one parsed by `_resolve_custom_pipeline_and_cls`.

**Therefore, it’s possible to introduce remote code into the repo between the two calls, bypassing the trust check.**

The race window is everything between the two Hub calls inside `download()`:

```python
# pipeline_utils.py:1636
config_file = hf_hub_download(...)   # ← sees commit A, trust check passes

# ... filenames processing, pattern building, pipeline_is_cached check ...
# ~~~ ATTACKER PUSHES COMMIT B HERE ~~~

# pipeline_utils.py:1778
cached_folder = snapshot_download(...)  # ← sees commit B, downloads pipeline.py
```

For the exploit, commit A carries a clean config with `_class_name` as a plain string, which causes `load_pipe_from_hub` to be `False` and the trust check to pass. Commit B changes `_class_name` to a list and adds `pipeline.py`:

**Commit A - `model_index.json`:**

```json
{
  "_class_name": "FluxPipeline",
  "_diffusers_version": "0.31.0"
}
```

**Commit B - `model_index.json`:**

```json
{
  "_class_name": ["pipeline", "FluxPipeline"],
  "_diffusers_version": "0.31.0"
}
```

When `from_pretrained` reads the snapshot after `download()` returns, `config["_class_name"]` is now a list, `pipeline.py` exists on disk (fetched by `snapshot_download`), and `_resolve_custom_pipeline_and_cls` resolves `custom_pipeline` to the local path of that file. `_get_pipeline_class` then imports it - with no trust check at this point in the code.

---

## PoC

1. Create a Hub repo with commit A’s `model_index.json` (plain string `_class_name`).
2. Run `DiffusionPipeline.from_pretrained("attacker/repo")` with a breakpoint set at `pipeline_utils.py:1778` (the `snapshot_download` call). This is for the window to be large enough to manually respond to it.
3. When execution pauses at the breakpoint, push commit B: update `model_index.json` to use a list `_class_name` and add `pipeline.py`.
4. Resume execution.
5. `snapshot_download` fetches commit B; `/tmp/pwned` is written during the subsequent `_get_pipeline_class` call.

---

## Constraints

- Does not apply when `revision` is pinned to a specific commit hash - both Hub calls resolve to the same content.
- Does not apply when loading from a local directory.
- If all expected files are already present in the local HF cache, `download()` returns early before reaching `snapshot_download` (line 1767 early-return), closing the race window. The exploit therefore requires a first (or forced) download.

---

## Exploitability

The window between the two calls is very short. Local testing resulted in a window of approximately ~0.5 seconds for the attacker to push the change. This is, of course, unfeasible to accomplish for each and every new download. However, given a popular repo with many downloads per day, one may achieve **statistical success** by changing the repo’s state every once in a while or every few seconds, with some percentage of downloaders falling on the exact window. 

---

## Impact

The vulnerability is a silent RCE - it allows arbitrary code to be loaded through the custom pipeline flow from a Hub repo, with no `custom_pipeline` or `trust_remote_code` kwargs. The `from_pretrained` call succeeds and returns a fully functional pipeline.

### 2. Diffusers has a `trust_remote_code` bypass via `custom_pipeline` and local custom components (CVE-2026-44513)
**Severidade:** HIGH

**Manifesto:** `botmodels/requirements.txt`

**Descrição:**
### Impact

A `trust_remote_code` bypass in `DiffusionPipeline.from_pretrained` allows arbitrary remote code execution despite the user passing `trust_remote_code=False` (or omitting it, which is the default). The vulnerability has three variants, all sharing the same root cause — the `trust_remote_code` gate was implemented inside `DiffusionPipeline.download()` rather than at the actual dynamic-module load site, so any code path that bypassed or short-circuited `download()` also bypassed the security check:

1. **Cross-repo `custom_pipeline`.** `DiffusionPipeline.from_pretrained('repoA', custom_pipeline='attacker/repoB', trust_remote_code=False)` — the gate evaluated against `repoA`'s file list rather than `repoB`'s, so `repoB`'s `pipeline.py` was loaded and executed.
2. **Local snapshot + Hub `custom_pipeline`.** `DiffusionPipeline.from_pretrained('/local/snapshot', custom_pipeline='attacker/repoB', trust_remote_code=False)` — the local-path branch never invoked `download()`, so the gate was never reached and remote code from `repoB` executed.
3. **Local snapshot with custom components.** `DiffusionPipeline.from_pretrained('/local/snapshot', trust_remote_code=False)` where the snapshot contains custom component files (e.g. `unet/my_unet_model.py`) referenced from `model_index.json` — same root cause; the local path skipped `download()` and custom component code executed.

Silent remote code execution on the victim's machine. Anyone calling `DiffusionPipeline.from_pretrained` with custom pipelines is impacted.

### Patches

Yes. Fixed in **diffusers 0.38.0** via [PR #13448](https://github.com/huggingface/diffusers/pull/13448). All users on versions `< 0.38.0` should upgrade:

```bash
pip install --upgrade "diffusers>=0.38.0"
```

The fix moves the `trust_remote_code` gate out of `DiffusionPipeline.download()` and into `get_cached_module_file` in `src/diffusers/utils/dynamic_modules_utils.py`, which is the actual chokepoint for every dynamic module load (local, Hub, or community mirror). All three variants now raise `ValueError` instead of executing untrusted code.

### Workarounds

If upgrading immediately is not possible:

- Only call `from_pretrained` with `pretrained_model_name_or_path`, `custom_pipeline`, and local snapshot directories from fully trusted sources that have been audited.
- Do not pass `custom_pipeline=` pointing at a Hub repository different from the primary `pretrained_model_name_or_path` before reading its `pipeline.py`.
- Before calling `from_pretrained` on a local snapshot, inspect the snapshot for unexpected `*.py` files, especially under component subdirectories (`unet/`, `scheduler/`, etc.) and at the snapshot root.

These are mitigations, not fixes — the only complete remediation is upgrading to 0.38.0.
